ppe-basics.title: Understanding PPE and Workplace Hazards
ppe-basics.content: Personal protective equipment (PPE) is anything worn to help prevent or reduce workplace injury or illness. PPE is the last line of defense between a worker and a hazard — it does not eliminate the hazard itself. Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.132, employers must assess the workplace to identify hazards and select appropriate PPE. PPE must match the specific task, environment, and exposure level. Damaged, inappropriate, or improperly used PPE can create a false sense of security without providing real protection.

ppe-requirements.title: General PPE Requirements and Training
ppe-requirements.content: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.132 requires employers to assess hazards, select appropriate PPE, and train all employees before they use it. Training must cover when PPE is necessary, what equipment is required, how to properly wear and adjust it, its limitations, and how to care for, maintain, and dispose of it. Employees must demonstrate understanding before using PPE on the job. Retraining is required when workplace conditions change, new equipment is introduced, or an employee shows inadequate knowledge. Employers remain responsible even when employees provide their own PPE.

eye-face-protection.title: Eye and Face Protection
eye-face-protection.content: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.133 requires suitable eye and face protection when employees face hazards from flying particles, sparks, chemical splashes, or intense light. Safety glasses protect against impact hazards; side shields are required when side impact is possible. Chemical splash hazards typically require goggles because they seal around the eyes, unlike safety glasses. Face shields add protection for arc flash, chemical splash, and heat but are generally worn over goggles, not instead of them. Welding and intense light tasks require filter lenses with appropriate shade numbers. Prescription eyewear is not a substitute unless designed for safety use.

respiratory-protection.title: Respiratory Protection
respiratory-protection.content: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.134 requires respirators when engineering controls alone cannot reduce airborne contaminants to safe levels. Respirator type must be matched to the specific contaminant, its concentration, and oxygen levels in the work area. Cartridges must be selected for the specific hazard — a cartridge rated for organic vapors will not protect against acid gases. Tight-fitting respirators require a proper seal; workers must pass fit testing before use. Medical clearance may be required. A poor seal allows contaminants to bypass the filter entirely, making respirator use ineffective.

head-protection.title: Head Protection
head-protection.content: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.135 requires protective helmets where there is a risk of head injury from falling objects, bumps, or electrical hazards. Hard hats must meet ANSI/ISEA Z89.1 standards and must be inspected before each use for cracks, dents, fraying suspension, or discoloration. Hard hats should be replaced after any significant impact even if no visible damage is present. Bump caps protect only against minor bumps and scrapes in confined areas — they must never be substituted for hard hats where falling object hazards exist. Stickers, paint, and drill holes can compromise a hard hat's structural integrity.

foot-protection.title: Foot Protection
foot-protection.content: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.136 requires protective footwear when employees are exposed to hazards such as falling or rolling objects, sharp objects, slippery surfaces, chemical splash, or electrical hazards. Safety shoes or boots with steel toes protect against impact and compression. Puncture-resistant midsoles are required where sharp objects such as nails or scrap metal may be underfoot. Slip-resistant soles are important on wet, oily, or icy surfaces. Chemical-resistant footwear is needed when handling corrosive or hazardous liquids. Foot protection must meet ASTM F2412 and F2413 standards.

electrical-ppe.title: Electrical Protective Equipment
electrical-ppe.content: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.137 governs rubber insulating gloves, sleeves, and other electrical protective equipment. These items must be tested and certified per ASTM standards before use and at regular intervals. Any defect — including punctures, cuts, ozone cracking, embedded foreign material, or swelling — requires the item to be removed from service immediately and sent for testing or disposal. Electrical protective equipment must be used with appropriate leather protectors over rubber gloves to prevent mechanical damage. Workers using electrical PPE must be trained on its limitations, inspection procedures, and care requirements.

hand-protection.title: Hand Protection
hand-protection.content: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.138 requires suitable hand protection when employees' hands face hazards such as skin absorption of harmful substances, cuts, lacerations, abrasions, punctures, burns, or extreme temperatures. No single glove material protects against all hazards — gloves must be selected for the specific chemical, temperature, or mechanical risk. Workers handling corrosive liquids must use chemically compatible gloves tested for that specific substance. Loose gloves must not be worn near rotating machinery where they could be caught. Gloves should be inspected before use and replaced when contaminated, damaged, or no longer effective.

ppe-maintenance.title: Inspecting, Maintaining, and Storing PPE
ppe-maintenance.content: All PPE must be inspected before each use. Any item that shows damage — cracks, tears, discoloration, missing components, contamination, or signs of wear — must be removed from service immediately and replaced. PPE should be cleaned per the manufacturer's instructions and stored away from heat, ultraviolet light, chemicals, and physical damage. Disposable PPE must not be reused. Storage areas should be clean, dry, and accessible. Workers should never assume PPE is functional because it was previously used without incident. Reporting missing or defective PPE to a supervisor is both a right and a responsibility.
